evals.prompt: I run devrel at Halcyon Metrics, a Series A observability startup in Lisbon. I've got 180,000 EUR approved for next year and I need to split it. The team is me (about 25 hours a week on devrel after my support rotation), a technical writer at 30 hours a week, and a designer who gives us maybe 6 hours a week. Salaries sit on a separate headcount line our VP Marketing owns. Our funded driver is self-serve developer adoption. Last year we ran 3 conferences, published 14 blog posts, and started a Discord. Can you give me the split across events, content, community, docs and tooling, and education?
evals.expected_output: A budget allocation stating both a cash envelope and an hours envelope, money sorted into four buckets, concentration into at most two pillars with the starved pillar named, a reserve, per-line owners with cash and hours, an unfunded list, an ordered cut list, and a short funder narrative.
expectations: States an hours envelope alongside the cash envelope, totalled from the three named people at 25, 30 and 6 hours per week.
Applies a deduction of between 20% and 30% to the hours envelope before planning against it, and gives the reason (support load, launches, incidents).
Sorts the money into committed, discretionary, borrowed and in-kind rather than treating all 180,000 EUR as allocatable.
States explicitly that the 180,000 EUR excludes staff salaries, and notes that this changes any comparison with other programs.
Funds at most two pillars above token level rather than splitting across all five pillars the user listed.
Names what the chosen concentration deliberately starves.
Holds between 10% and 20% of discretionary spend as an unallocated reserve.
Labels the reserve percentage as a self-set starting point rather than an industry standard.
Gives every funded line an owner who is one of the three named people, never 'the team' or 'devrel'.
Gives every funded line both a cash figure and an hours figure.
Flags any line whose hours exceed the hours envelope as unfunded regardless of its cash.
Produces both an unfunded list and an ordered cut list, and neither is empty.
Closes with a funder narrative of at most five sentences containing no devrel jargon.
Tags every percentage or threshold it states as sourced, program baseline, or self-set.

evals.prompt: Our CFO looked at next year's devrel plan and said 40% on events is way above industry norms and we should cut it to 15%. We're Brightforge, we sell an enterprise API gateway, deals are six figures and always involve a security architect plus a platform lead signing off before procurement. Budget is $420K excluding salaries. Who's right here, and what's the actual industry benchmark for event spend?
evals.expected_output: The published survey figure quoted with all its caveats and refused as a target, plus a decision made on Brightforge's own funded driver and enterprise buying motion.
expectations: Names the published figure as a mean of 41.1% of program budget going to events, attributed to a named 2024 developer relations survey.
States the sample size of n=47 for that allocation-split question.
States that the published shares sum to more than 100% (104.5%), so respondents answered on inconsistent bases.
States that the published category set omits community, tooling, education and OSS sponsorship, so a pillar allocation cannot be mapped onto it one-to-one.
Refuses to present 41.1% as a correct or target event share.
States that roughly 60% of surveyed program budgets exclude salaries, so the published split and Brightforge's $420K are not directly comparable.
Decides the question on Brightforge's funded driver and adoption motion rather than on the survey figure.
Identifies Brightforge's motion as company or enterprise buying, using the six-figure deals and the named approvers as the evidence.
States that an enterprise buying motion promotes field-and-events to the top of both the value and the efficiency ordering.
Does not invent any figure for devrel spend as a share of revenue or of marketing spend.
Tags the 41.1% figure as sourced, and keeps it distinct from any self-set number it proposes.
Recommends a defensible event share for Brightforge without describing that share as an industry norm.

evals.prompt: Finance just told me to take 20% out of devrel by Friday, and they've hinted a 40% scenario might follow. Current year at Northwind Data, $300K discretionary: conference booths $90K, agency content pipeline $70K, docs and samples maintenance $55K, Discord community plus champions $40K, OSS sponsorships $25K, newsletter sponsorships $20K. The docs line is what keeps four SDK sample repos green in CI. I've defended the agency content pipeline at two consecutive reviews as our long-game bet. What should I cut?
evals.expected_output: Two ordered cut scenarios (20% and 40%), each removal carrying a one-sentence consequence, rented reach going first, the actively-decaying docs line protected, and the twice-protected compounding line held back from being cut first.
expectations: Produces an ordered cut list rather than a flat percentage trim applied to every line.
Builds both a 20% and a 40% scenario, with the 40% scenario containing the 20% removals.
Attaches a one-sentence consequence to every removal.
Cuts rented reach first, taking newsletter sponsorships and sponsorship depth before compounding or foundational lines.
Protects the docs and SDK sample maintenance line, cutting it last or not at all.
Justifies protecting that line because its neglect is actively wrong (broken samples, stale docs) rather than merely invisible.
States that the cut order is the efficiency ordering read from the bottom, not a ranking by cash size.
Does not rank the pillars against each other by cost per outcome unit anywhere in the answer.
Does not put the agency content pipeline first on the chopping block, on the grounds that a compounding line protected across two periods cannot be the first thing dropped.
Warns that a team volunteering no order gets a flat percentage applied to every line, which starves compounding work first.
Notes that roughly a quarter of surveyed programs lost budget in a single year, so a cut is a normal planning case rather than a crisis.
States which lines must be protected, not only which lines go.
Names what capability is lost in the 40% scenario, not only the dollar amount removed.

evals.prompt: Honest question: I've asked three times and nobody will tell me what our devrel budget actually is. I'm at Verdanix, about 120 people, B2B data pipeline tooling. My manager says 'just tell me what you need' and finance says 'ask your manager'. I need to plan Q1 through Q4. Do I just guess a number and build the plan around it?
evals.expected_output: Reframes the missing number as the majority case, switches the deliverable to a list of questions with owners and dates plus a percentage-based provisional split, and still states an hours envelope.
expectations: Tells the user this is the majority case, citing that about a third of surveyed practitioners cannot state their budget and roughly another sixth have no set budget at all.
Refuses to invent a currency figure for Verdanix's budget.
Does not produce a benchmark budget derived from headcount, revenue or company stage.
Switches the deliverable to a list of questions that must get answered, each with a named owner to ask and a date to get it by.
Produces a provisional allocation expressed in percentages rather than in currency.
States that the percentage split survives whatever absolute number eventually comes back.
Asks whether the number, when it arrives, includes staff salaries.
Asks who signs the budget off and when the cycle locks.
Asks what is already committed under contract and for how long.
Still states an hours envelope, because capacity is knowable even when cash is not.
Notes that the reporting line usually determines who signs the budget, and that no single reporting line holds a majority in the published survey.

evals.prompt: Building the board deck for our devrel program at Caldera Systems. The board wants three numbers: what percentage of ARR we should be spending on developer relations, what our cost per developer reached should be, and what the normal headcount-to-budget ratio is for a devrel team at Series B. We're at $14M ARR, 3 devrel people, $260K program budget. Give me the benchmarks and where we land against them.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to supply any of the three benchmarks, an explanation that no quotable industry figure exists for them, the program's own prior period offered as the only legitimate baseline, and a defensible alternative for the deck.
expectations: Refuses to state a benchmark for devrel spend as a percentage of ARR or revenue.
Refuses to state a benchmark for cost per developer reached.
Refuses to state a benchmark headcount-to-budget ratio.
States plainly that no quotable industry figure exists for these, rather than producing a plausible one.
Does not compute Caldera's own ratios and then present them as a comparison against an industry figure.
Offers the program's own prior period as the only legitimate baseline for each of the three numbers.
Where no prior-period baseline exists, proposes funding the line as an experiment with a fixed window and a kill date instead of a number.
Also refuses to supply a recommended split across community, tooling, education or sponsorship.
Offers the board deck an alternative it can defend, such as line-level thresholds derived from Caldera's own baseline.
Tags any number it does state as sourced, program baseline, or self-set.
Warns that a specific-sounding figure gets quoted back for years after the guess behind it is forgotten.
Does not describe any self-set figure it proposes as a standard or a benchmark.

evals.prompt: We're launching our v3 platform at Stilwater on March 14th, which is about ten weeks out, and I have $120K of unspent devrel budget that has to go out this fiscal year or we lose it. My shortlist: sign a content agency to run our blog, build a certification program for our partner integrators, buy three newsletter sponsorships, and refresh the quickstart. I want the launch to land loudly. What gets funded?
evals.expected_output: Lines whose latency runs past March 14 deleted on latency grounds with the published setup-cost and lead-time figures cited, rented reach promoted, the quickstart funded, and the deleted lines named with the constraint that removed them.
expectations: Treats March 14 as the binding constraint on which lines can be funded at all.
Deletes the content agency line for this period on latency grounds rather than on cost grounds.
Cites roughly 8 to 9 weeks from concept to publication for an outsourced piece, attributed to a published account of an agency content pipeline.
Cites roughly six months of a director's own time to build that pipeline before it produced at volume.
Deletes the certification program because its build runs a quarter or more, past the launch date.
Promotes rented reach, specifically the newsletter sponsorships, because the result must land inside the period.
Funds the quickstart refresh, whose latency fits inside ten weeks.
Says which answer or constraint moved which line.
States that a budget which must be spent this period or is lost promotes rented reach and demotes anything whose first readable signal lands after the lock date.
States that paid distribution stops working the day it stops being paid, so it belongs in the campaign horizon and never in the compounding one.
Names the certification program's permanent recurring obligations, such as item security, cheating response and recertification cycles, if it is ever funded.
Puts the deleted lines on a named ruled-out list with the constraint that removed them, rather than at the bottom of a ranking.

evals.prompt: Aldergate went fully remote and our COO put a hard freeze on all conference travel. It's not a budget thing, it's policy, and it isn't lifting this year. I've got 95,000 GBP discretionary for devrel. I still want you to show me all the options ranked so I can see what we're giving up. Also, I'd love a certification program but there's no way we can staff it, our one advocate is already at capacity.
evals.expected_output: Field-and-events and the certification program deleted outright onto a ruled-out list with their constraints named, a separate unfunded list, and the remaining shapes ranked on effort axes with the starved option named.
expectations: Deletes the field-and-events shape outright rather than ranking it last.
Names the travel policy as the constraint that removed field-and-events.
Puts field-and-events on a ruled-out list kept separate from the unfunded list.
Also rules out the certification program, naming the advocate's capacity ceiling as the constraint.
States that an effort ceiling below what a line needs deletes that line rather than demoting it.
Explains that a ruled-out line parked at the bottom of a ranking reappears as scope the next time the envelope moves.
States that a ruled-out line returns only if the constraint lifts, unlike an unfunded line.
Produces a non-empty unfunded list distinct from the ruled-out list, with one line each on what would have to change to fund it.
Ranks the remaining shapes against each other, not against the deleted one.
Ranks them on effort axes such as hours, setup latency and exit cost, never on cash.
Names what the resulting order starves and the condition that would promote it.
Does not propose working around the travel freeze with a smaller or cheaper event line.

evals.prompt: I pulled last year's numbers at Ravencourt and I want you to rank our pillars by ROI so I know what to fund. Events: $88K for 140 qualified conversations, so $629 each. Content: $54K for 22 published pieces, $2,454 a piece. Community: $31K and 1,840 answered questions, $17 each. Docs and samples: $46K, and honestly I can't put a number on it. Community is clearly the winner at $17 a unit. Should I move money out of content and events into community?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to rank pillars by cost per unit, the two legitimate cost-per-unit comparisons named, an effort-based ranking instead, the outcome-share versus budget-share comparison offered, and the unmeasured docs line treated as a visibility problem.
expectations: Refuses to rank the four pillars against each other by cost per outcome unit.
States that the units measure different things, so the comparison is invalid rather than merely imprecise.
States that the pillar easiest to instrument wins such a ranking regardless of its actual value.
Names the two comparisons where cost per unit stays legitimate: the same pillar across periods, and the same pillar across options.
Refuses to recommend moving money into community on the strength of the $17 figure.
Ranks the pillars on effort instead, using hours, setup latency and exit cost, expressed in magnitudes.
Does not use a cash figure as the denominator of any ranking it produces.
Offers the outcome-share versus budget-share comparison as the legitimate cross-pillar adjustment, and explains that it works because it compares two ratios rather than two costs.
Says to fund up where outcome share exceeds budget share and the audience is still under-served.
Says to question any pillar whose budget share has outrun its outcome share for two consecutive periods.
Treats the docs line's missing number as a visibility problem rather than as evidence the line is weak.
Warns that growing spend on an outcome nobody can read buys a renewal argument, not a result.
Notes community's unusually high exit cost, where winding it down damages trust in a way a cancelled sponsorship does not, before recommending any increase.

evals.prompt: Let me lay out what I've got at Fenwick Labs for FY27. Total pot: $340K. That includes a three-year conference sponsorship we signed in 2025 at $48K a year with one year left and a 90-day notice clause, a community platform licence at $9K renewing in November, and about $60K that Demand Gen spends on developer dinners which our VP told me I can count as mine this year. Plus our staff engineers give us maybe 5 hours a week for reviews. So I've got $340K to play with. Where do I put it?
evals.expected_output: The $340K split into committed, discretionary, borrowed and in-kind, the signed contract treated as a renew-or-notice decision, the Demand Gen money attributed to its real owner and excluded from the discretionary total, and a notice-date reallocation trigger written.
expectations: Separates the $340K into committed, discretionary, borrowed and in-kind rather than treating it as one allocatable figure.
Classifies the three-year conference sponsorship and the community platform licence as committed, not discretionary.
States the discretionary figure that is actually being allocated, net of the committed lines.
Treats the conference contract as a renew-or-notice decision keyed to its 90-day notice date, not as a line to re-justify mid-contract.
Records the November renewal date for the community platform licence as its own notice decision.
Classifies the $60K of Demand Gen spend as borrowed, names Demand Gen as its owner, and marks it as outside Fenwick's control.
States that no critical line may depend on the borrowed money.
Classifies the 5 hours a week of staff-engineer review as in-kind, with a hard ceiling and no invoice.
Warns that the other team re-planning can make a borrowed line vanish mid-period.
Notes that more than one team performing devrel work means a single program budget understates total company spend on the function.
Adds a reallocation trigger for the moment a committed contract reaches its notice date.
Does not include the borrowed $60K inside the discretionary total it then splits.

evals.prompt: Help me write the success criteria for next year's devrel lines at Sablecourt. My draft: Discord should hit 10,000 members, the blog should become the top Google result for 'event-driven architecture', conference booths should generate strong pipeline, and docs should just stay current. We've never really tracked any of this, our analytics only got set up in August and nobody owns the numbers. I want targets I can take to my VP.
evals.expected_output: Aspiration-derived targets rejected, baseline-less lines converted into experiments with kill dates, pillar-native outcome units assigned, the four-point readability score applied and failed, and affected lines held flat with the increment spent on visibility.
expectations: Rejects thresholds derived from aspiration rather than from a baseline the program already has.
Points out that Sablecourt has no baseline for these lines, so most of them cannot carry a number yet.
Converts baseline-less lines into experiments with a fixed window and a written 'we will know X by date Y' statement instead of a number.
Rejects a raw Discord member count as an outcome unit, because joins can be bought without producing a single answered question.

Gives each pillar an outcome unit from that pillar's own vocabulary, such as cost per qualified conversation for events, cost per published-and-reviewed piece for content, and cost per answered question or active contributor for community.
Rejects 'stay current' and 'strong pipeline' as thresholds because they carry no unit and no number, so the line renews by default.

Scores the program 1 to 3 on each of four readability points: the outcome is instrumented at all, the instrumentation predates the spend, someone owns the number, and there is an agreed attribution story.
Notes that Sablecourt's instrumentation does not predate the spend and nobody owns the numbers, so the score falls below half marks.
Holds the affected lines flat and spends the increment on visibility first, rather than growing a line nobody can read.
Labels the four-point score and its cut-off as a self-set gate rather than an industry standard.
Frames every threshold as repeatable and cheap to apply rather than statistically rigorous.
Explains that a threshold defended as proof invites an attribution argument that devrel measurement cannot win.
Gives every line a review date and a written miss action, both set before the money is spent.

evals.prompt: Skip the process, I just need the numbers. Kessler Interactive, $250K devrel budget for next year, four-person team, we make a game engine SDK. Developers find us individually and start on the free tier, then their studios upgrade once a project ships. Give me the table with the percentages per pillar and I'll take it from there.
evals.expected_output: Explicit brainstorming mode with two or three whole-budget candidates rather than one table, each presented with six stated properties, a recommendation, a request for the shape to be agreed before pricing, and the motion identified as individual adoption.
expectations: Does not hand over a single pillar percentage table on the first pass.
Says explicitly that it is in brainstorming mode before proposing anything.
Builds two or three whole-budget candidates rather than one.

Presents each candidate with the pillar it over-invests in, its three largest lines, what it deliberately starves, the hours it needs, the earliest signal it is working, and the conditions under which it is the wrong shape.
Recommends one candidate and says why.
Asks the budget owner to pick a shape before anything is priced in detail, warning that a wrong shape propagates into every line below it.
Identifies Kessler's motion as individual-developer adoption from the description of how developers arrive.
States that individual adoption sends money toward discoverability and time-to-first-success rather than toward field presence.
States that any line whose share nobody can explain is zero-based this cycle, whichever budgeting mode is chosen.
Names community-led as the shape the default efficiency order starves, together with the conditions that would promote it.
Applies a two-pillar concentration limit rather than spreading across every pillar, and justifies it on the consistency threshold below which devrel work does not pay.
Does not adopt last year's split as the starting point without it being explained.
Labels any archetype percentage weights it quotes as illustrative starting points for an argument rather than benchmarks.

evals.prompt: At Pallas Fabric we depend hard on one Rust crate that basically is our storage layer. One maintainer, and if they walk we're in trouble. I've got $40K for open source this year. My plan is $50 a month across our top 60 dependencies because that spreads goodwill widest per dollar, and then whatever's left over goes wherever. My CFO will love the coverage number. Sound right?
evals.expected_output: Breadth identified as the efficiency winner but the value loser, depth promoted for the critical-path crate with the promotion condition stated, hours priced for the line, the procurement invoice floor flagged, and the coverage count refused as an outcome unit.
expectations: States that breadth beats depth on efficiency but loses to it on value, so a program ranked on ratio alone never funds depth.
Recommends promoting depth for the single Rust crate, because it carries the product's critical path.
States the second condition that promotes depth: a funded driver of supply-chain exposure rather than goodwill.
Contrasts the two motions' effort, with breadth a setup pass and near-zero after it, and depth days of diligence plus a standing relationship.
States what depth buys that breadth does not: a named maintainer who answers, rather than coverage and goodwill.
Prices hours for the sponsorship line, covering dependency selection, maintainer contact and diligence, invoicing and vendor onboarding, renewal reviews and internal reporting.
Warns that some funding platforms enforce an invoice minimum for procurement-routed payments, which sets a floor on any line routed through purchase orders.
Names the exit cost of a sponsorship: the return sits inside a surface someone else controls.
Does not rank the sponsorship line against another pillar by cost per unit.
Sets the depth portion up as an experiment with a kill date if no baseline exists for it.
Refuses the dependency coverage count as the line's outcome unit.
